summary: RFC 5965 defines the Abuse Reporting Format (ARF) for machine-readable email feedback. This applicability statement describes common ways to use it to report both abuse and authentication failures, as a basis for procedures by mailbox providers and senders.

eli5.summary: When someone gets junk mail, they can send a standard complaint form. This explains how to use that form well.

subtitle: Practical advice on when, where and how to send machine-readable email abuse and authentication-failure reports.

tldr.problem: The Abuse Reporting Format (ARF) says how to structure a feedback report, but not who should send one, to whom, or what to put in it. Reports to strangers can waste time or be used to flood a victim.
tldr.mechanism: This applicability statement splits use into solicited abuse reports, unsolicited abuse reports and automatic authentication-failure reports, and gives SHOULD and MUST rules for each, such as which fields to include and where to send.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5965 and gives mailbox providers, senders and report recipients a common set of practices.

today: RFC 6650 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5965. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why an Applicability Statement
sections.content:
The Abuse Reporting Format (ARF) from RFC 5965 was first built for two cases: large email operators reporting to each other, or to the network access operators of end users, and those same operators reporting to others such as bulk senders. In both cases a report is usually triggered by a person, for example by clicking a "report spam" button in a mail client.

This document, RFC 6650, gives direction for using ARF for abuse reports and for authentication-failure reports. Its stated goal is to stop recurrences of abuse while automating reporting as far as practical, to reduce the work of a site's abuse team. Many of its guidelines come from the principles in RFC 6449.

Five feedback types are registered at the time of writing. Only two are covered here, abuse and auth-failure, because they see enough use in practice. The others (fraud, other, not-spam) are described as too new or too seldom used.
sections.eli5: There is already a standard complaint form for bad email. This paper is the instruction sheet for filling it in and sending it sensibly.

sections.title: Solicited and Unsolicited Reports
sections.content:
The RFC defines a Mailbox Provider as an organization that accepts, stores and offers access to email messages for end users. It separates two kinds of report.

Solicited reports are the original and still by far the most common use. Two mail systems make a private agreement to exchange abuse reports, usually triggered by recipients manually marking messages as spam.

Unsolicited reports go between parties who do not know each other and have no prior agreement about what the reports mean. The constraints on addresses, topics and handling are very different, so the RFC treats the two cases separately.
sections.eli5: A solicited report is a note you send to a friend who asked for it. An unsolicited one goes to a stranger, so you have to be much more careful.

sections.title: Solicited Abuse Reports
sections.content:
A Mailbox Provider usually learns about abuse through a "report spam" button in the mail user agent. How the message gets from that client to the provider's ARF system is not defined by any standard. Reports are formatted per RFC 5965 and sent as ordinary email, typically over SMTP.

Providers SHOULD NOT send reports to addresses that have not explicitly requested them. Reports SHOULD use Feedback-Type: abuse, and SHOULD include the optional fields Original-Mail-From, Arrival-Date, Source-IP and Original-Rcpt-To when their values are available. User-identifiable data MAY be obscured as described in RFC 6590.

Receivers MUST be able to accept ARF reports as email over SMTP. An automated system MUST NOT reject a report in the SMTP sense solely because of an unknown Feedback-Type; it can set such reports aside for manual handling. Receivers MUST also accept reports that have obscured user-identifiable data.
sections.eli5: If a friend asked to hear about junk mail, you tell them with a standard form, include the useful details, and they have to accept it even if the form has a new kind of label.

sections.title: Unsolicited Abuse Reports
sections.content:
Handling unsolicited reports costs the receiver real effort, so senders are told to be selective. Feedback Providers MUST provide a way for recipients to ask that no further reports be sent, though the RFC notes that no standard mechanism for this exists and all current ones are out-of-band. Senders SHOULD expect their reports to pass SPF and/or DKIM checks, so they are credible.

Senders SHOULD NOT send reports that cannot be acted on, and SHOULD NOT report all mail from a sender merely because some was abusive. Reports based only on inline content analysis that "looks like" spam SHOULD NOT be sent. Complaints from end users and mail delivered to spam-trap or honeypot addresses are far more likely to be accurate and MAY be sent. If SPF evaluation gave "Fail", "SoftFail", "TempError" or "PermError", a report SHOULD NOT be sent to the RFC5321.MailFrom domain, since use of that domain may not have been authorized.

Where to send is guesswork. Good candidates are abuse contacts in WHOIS records for the relaying IP address, the domain from a PTR lookup, or the abuse@domain role address. Reports SHOULD NOT go to uninvolved parties, such as every Autonomous System operator along the path, or to the abusive party's own reporting address unless it is known to be responsive.

Reports SHOULD use Feedback-Type: abuse and include the same four optional fields. Senders SHOULD put all needed information in the human-readable first text/plain part, because some recipients can only read that. They SHOULD NOT generate reports for which no reply can be received.
sections.eli5: Do not mail complaints to strangers who cannot do anything about them. Send them only to someone who can help, make the note easy to read, and give a real address for answers.

sections.title: Automatic Authentication Failure Reports
sections.content:
Some reports are generated by machines rather than people, for example when a message fails an email authentication check. RFC 6651 and RFC 6652 are named as examples. The rules here are somewhat smaller because many abuse-report issues do not apply.

Generators MUST select recipients from data provided by willing report receivers and MUST NOT select them by heuristics. If the message being checked is itself an ARF message, a report MUST NOT be generated automatically.

To avoid amplification attacks and mail loops, the envelope sender MUST be chosen so that no feedback reports are issued in response to the report. When SMTP is used, MAIL FROM SHOULD use the null reverse-path, MAIL FROM:<>. Reports SHOULD use Feedback-Type: auth-failure and include the same four optional fields when available.
sections.eli5: A robot that reports problems must only write to people who asked, never reply to another robot's report, and use a return address that stops endless back-and-forth.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Readers are urged to review the security sections of RFC 5965 and RFC 6449. This RFC adds several specific risks.

  • Forgeries: a provider that relays user complaints directly could be tricked into complaining about a message the user never got. Reports can be forged as easily as ordinary email, so they should themselves be signed with something like DKIM and/or authorized by something like SPF.
  • Amplification: ignoring the envelope sender advice can enable amplification denial-of-service attacks.
  • Automatic generation: automated reports can mean far larger volumes. The extension mechanisms are meant mainly for development and debugging, not prolonged forensic use.
  • Multiple incidents: an attacker who knows a host reports certain incidents could forge many messages to flood a victim. The incident count in ARF offers limited mitigation, for example reporting each of the first ten incidents, then every tenth up to 100, then every 100th up to 1000. This lowers the quality of reporting.

Other rate limits are suggested, such as pausing after a temporary failure response or agreeing a hard limit with a receiver.
sections.eli5: Bad guys can fake complaints or trick a computer into sending a flood of them at someone. So senders should prove who they are and slow down when there are lots.

viz.caption: THE THREE REPORT CASES IN RFC 6650

cells: User action such as a report spam button
Heuristics such as WHOIS and abuse@domain
Data from willing receivers, never heuristics
